label: def:ltdregion
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ltdregion}
    A \textbf{\emph{locally top-depth component}} $U$ of a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ is a connected, open, saturated subset, such that all leaves in $U$ have the same depth, which is finite and greater than the depth of any leaf in $\overline{U}$.
head: environment

label: lem:top depth is fibered
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $U$ is a top-depth component. A combination of Lemma 9.1.3 and Theorem 9.1.4 in \cite{candel_foliations_1999}  implies that the leaf space $\mathcal{L}$ of $\mathcal{F}\left.\right|_U$ is a closed 1-manifold. The key observation is that all the leaves in $U$ are proper and have trivial germinal holonomy, so a neighborhood of each leaf of $U$ is a trivial product, giving the local Euclidean structure.
    
    Note that although the results in \cite{candel_foliations_1999} are stated for $C^2$ foliations, the primary place the assumption is used is to guarantee that the leaves of $U$ are proper, local minimal sets. However, by our hypothesis, all leaves of $U$ are proper and so the rest of the proofs of both results hold verbatim.

    The leaf space $\mathcal{L}$ will be a circle if and only if $U$ is not a trivially foliated product (\cite[Lemma 9.1.6]{candel_foliations_1999}), which follows from the definition of a locally top-depth component.

    On the other hand, suppose $U$ is a connected open saturated set in a finite depth foliation which is not a locally top-depth component. We claim that $\mathcal F$ does not restrict to a fibration over $S^1$ on $U$. If not all leaves of $U$ are homeomorphic, or if not all leaves in $U$ have the same depth, this is clear. So suppose $U$ satisfies all the required conditions except that there is some leaf $S$ in $\overline{U} \setminus U$ which has depth equal to the depth of leaves in $U$ (by definition, $S$ cannot have greater depth than $U$). In particular, this shows that the leaves of $U$ do not spiral onto $S$. Then $S$ is homeomorphic to the leaves of $U$ by an isotopy along flowlines of an auxiliary transverse flow. This is a consequence of the Dippolito Semistability Theorem, see \cite[Theorem 5.3.4]{candel_foliations_1999}. 
    
    The same argument as above shows that the leaf space of $\mathcal {F} \left.\right|_U$ is a 1-manifold. But $S$ provides an endpoint compactifying the leaf space of $U$ on one side. This shows that the leaf space is homeomorphic to an open interval, not $S^1$.
head: environment

label: lem:depth1octopus
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: lem:juncturesinproduct
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:juncturesinproduct}
    Let $U$ be a locally top-depth component which is a product region, and let $\Sigma_\pm$ be the positive and negative boundary components of $\widehat{U}$. Then $j^+(\Sigma_-) = -j^-(\Sigma_+)$, and up to topological conjugacy $\widehat{U}$ is obtained by shearing the product foliation $\Sigma_- \times [0,1]$ along any product annulus or infinite strip $\gamma \times [0,1]$, where $\gamma$ is a connected, embedded 1-manifold in $\Sigma_-$ Poincar\'e dual to $j^+(\Sigma_-)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that $\widehat{U}$ is a foliated interval bundle homeomorphic to $\Sigma_- \times [0, 1]$, i.e. under a homeomorphism, the pullback foliation on $\widehat U$ is transverse to the vertical foliation by intervals in $\Sigma_-\times [0,1]$. Thus, the foliation is determined up to conjugacy by the induced holonomy representation 
	\[\rho: \pi_1(\Sigma_1, x) \to \operatorname{Homeo}_+([0, 1]),
	\]
	where $x$ is some basepoint. Moreover, since $U$ is a locally top-depth component, it has trivial holonomy, and hence $\rho$ has the property that $\rho(g)$ is the identity if and only if $\rho(g)$ has an interior fixed point.
    
    From this we see as follows that $\rho(g)$ is abelian and determined precisely by $j^+(\Sigma_-)$. Let $\{x_i \in (0, 1)\}_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a monotonically decreasing sequence so that $(x,x_i)\in\Sigma_-\times[0,1]$ is contained in the same leaf $L$ for all $i$. Then for sufficiently large $i$ and any $g, h \in \pi_1(\Sigma_-, x)$, there is some $n$ so that 
    \[
    \rho([g,h])(x_i) = x_{i + nj^+([g, h])} = x_i
    \]
    for $j^+ = j^+(\Sigma_-)$.

    We see that $\rho$ is conjugate to the representation $j^+(\Sigma)$ under an identification of $(0,1)$ and $\mathbb{R}$ taking the points $L \cap x \times (0,1)$ to the integers. The same argument shows that $\rho$ is determined by $j^-(\Sigma_+)$, except that loops which decrease points go to loops that increase points under the identification. Hence $j^+(\Sigma_-) = -j^-(\Sigma_+)$. 

    Moreover, a foliation on $\Sigma_- \times [0,1]$ determined by shearing along a curve $\gamma$ representing the juncture has a conjugate holonomy map, showing that the foliations are conjugate.
head: environment

title: Convention
body_md: For the rest of the paper, let $M$ be a closed, orientable, atoroidal 3-manifold, and let $\mathcal F$ be a coorientable 2-dimensional foliation on $M$.
head: environment

label: thm:locallytopdepthclosing
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:locallytopdepthclosing}
	Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth, and let $\varphi$ be a transverse flow. If $\mathcal F$ contains a locally top depth component $U$ that is not a product region, then $\varphi$ contains a closed orbit.
head: environment

label: lem:depth one is endperiodic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:depth one is endperiodic}
    Let $U$ be a depth one region of a depth one foliation, and let $\widehat U$ be the path closure of $U$. Then $\widehat U$ with its foliation is homeomorphic to a compactified endperiodic mapping torus with its natural foliation. A representative of the monodromy is given by the first return map of any flow transverse to the foliation.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ be as above with $L$ a leaf in $U$. By Lemma \ref{lem:top depth is fibered}, $U$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $L$. Let $\varphi$ be a flow transverse to the depth one foliation. What remains to be shown is just that the monodromy is endperiodic. 

    Each end of $L$ spirals onto a depth zero leaf $\Sigma$ in $\partial\widehat U$ in a \textbf{\emph{spiralling neighborhood}}, as in \cite[Section 6]{CC81}. In particular, in some regular neighborhood $N\cong \Sigma\times I$ of $\Sigma$ in $\widehat U$, the restriction of $L$ to $N$ looks like an oriented cut and paste of copies of $\Sigma$ of the form $\Sigma\times\{1/n\}$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with an annulus $\gamma\times\mathcal{I}$ for $\gamma$ some essential simple closed curve in $\Sigma$. Take $N$ small enough so that $\varphi$ is trivial, and then from this picture one can see the endperiodic nature of the monodromy.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $f\colon L\to L$ be spun pseudo-Anosov, and let $g$ be an endperiodic map homotopic to $f$. Then for all $n\geq 0$, $g$ has at least as many periodic points of period $n$ as $f$.
head: environment
name: Landry--Minsky--Taylor

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $f$ be a spun pseudo-Anosov map. Then $f$ has no periodic points if and only if $f$ is a translation.
head: environment
name: Landry--Minsky--Taylor

label: lem:translation mapping torus
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:translation mapping torus}
	An endperiodic map $f\colon L\to L$ is homotopic to a translation if and only if 
	\[
	\overline{M_f}\cong \Sigma\times I,
	\]
	for $\Sigma$ a closed surface.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First assume $f$ as above is a translation. Then every point in $L$ is both positively and negatively escaping under $f$, so the suspension flow on $\overline{M_f}$ gives it an interval bundle structure. Thus, it must be a product. 
	
	On the other hand, if $\overline{M_f}$ is a product for some map $f$, $f$ must be homotopic to a translation  -- this can be seen by considering the vertical transverse flow and applying Lemma \ref{lem:depth one is endperiodic}.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:locallytopdepthclosingagain}
	Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth, and let $\varphi$ be a transverse flow. If $\mathcal F$ contains a locally top depth component $U$ that is not a product region, then $\varphi$ contains a closed orbit.

label: lem:reebcomponentforces
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:reebcomponentforces}
    If $\mathcal F$ has a Reeb component, every flow $\varphi$ transverse to $\mathcal F$ has a closed orbit contained in each Reeb component.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal F$ contains a Reeb component. Let $\varphi$ be a flow transverse to $\mathcal F$, and let $L$ be a planar leaf in the interior of the Reeb component. Observe $L$ is a fiber of a plane bundle over $S^1$. By reversing the direction of $\varphi$ if necessary, we assume that the flow points into the Reeb component along its boundary. The flow $\varphi$ defines a first return map $f: L \to L$. This is not an endperiodic map as $L$ has only one end; however, $f$ still has controlled end behavior. 
	
	Let $\gamma$ be a simple closed curve in the boundary torus $T$ of the Reeb component which is Poincar\'e dual to the juncture class. Then cutting $L$ along a small flowout annulus of $\gamma$ along $\varphi$ separates the complement of a compact disk $D_0$ in $L$ into an infinite union $\{A_i\}$ of annuli glued along their boundaries, which we order by distance from $D_0$. Moreover, for an annulus $A_N$ sufficiently far from $D_0$, $f$ takes $A_N$ to $A_{N-1}$, and so defines a map on the compact disk $D = D_0 \cup A_1 \cup ... \cup A_N$. This map has a fixed point by Brouwer's fixed point theorem \cite{brouwer1911abbildung}. This gives the desired periodic orbit of $\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth, and let $\varphi$ be a transverse flow. Since $M$ is atoroidal, if $\mathcal F$ is not taut, then it contains a Reeb component. In this case, Lemma \ref{lem:reebcomponentforces} applies and produces a closed orbit of $\varphi$.
	
Suppose instead that $\mathcal F$ is taut and contains a locally top depth component $U$ that is not a product region. Note that since $\mathcal F$ is taut, the inclusion of $U$ into $M$ is $\pi_1$-injective. Since $M$ is atoroidal, $U$ must then be as well.	
	
Let $i:N \to M$ be the sutured manifold from Lemma \ref{lem:depth1octopus}. Let $L$ be a leaf of $i^*\mathcal{F}$. Then $L$ is depth 1 in $N$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:depth one is endperiodic}, the pullback flow $\varphi_N$ on $N$ defines an endperiodic first return homeomorphism $f_\varphi: L \to L$. The flow $\varphi$ has a closed orbit in the interior of $N$ if and only if $f_\varphi$ has a periodic orbit.

The leaf $L$ will in general have boundary components, which may not be compact. If $L$ has a noncompact boundary component, that boundary component must have one end escape out an attracting end and the other escape out a repelling end. If so, insert an infinite strip of genus along each noncompact boundary component to obtain a surface $L'$. Extend the homeomorphism $f_\varphi$ to each strip of genus via a translation map to obtain a map $f'_\varphi$. If $L$ has no noncompact boundary components, let $L'=L$ and $f'_\varphi=f_\varphi$.

Now double $L'$ along its boundary to obtain the infinite-type surface $DL'$. Note that $DL'$ has all ends nonplanar, and the doubled map 
\[
Df'_\varphi\colon DL'\to DL'
\]
is endperiodic.
    


    We claim $Df'_\varphi$ is atoroidal. Suppose it is not. Then there is a finite set of essential closed curves $\gamma_i$, $1 \leq i \leq k$ in $DL'$ which are permuted by $Df'_\varphi$ up to isotopy. Put each $\gamma_i$ in minimal position with respect to $\partial L$, viewed as a system of essential simple closed curves and properly embedded arcs within $DL'$. Note that $\partial L$ decomposes $DL'$ into two copies of $L$, denoted $L_0$ and $L_1$, and a collection of infinite strips of genus.
    
    First note that no $\gamma_i$ can lie entirely in $L_0$ or $L_1$ inside $DL'$. This is because $Df'_\varphi$ preserves $L_0$ and $L_1$, and a periodic curve in $L$ under $f_\varphi$ would contradict the fact that $U$ is atoroidal.
    
    On the other hand, no $\gamma_i$ can intersect one of the infinite strips of genus. Suppose some $\gamma_i$ did, and let $\alpha$ be an auxiliary curve entirely inside the infinite strip and with positive geometric intersection number with $\gamma_i$. Since $Df'_\varphi$ acts on the strip as a translation, for large $N$ we have 
    \[
    i(\alpha,Df'^N_\varphi(\gamma_i))=0.
    \]
    Thus, $Df'^N_\varphi(\gamma_i)$ and $\gamma_i$ cannot be homotopic.
    
    Finally, no $\gamma_i$ can intersect a compact boundary component of $L_0$ or $L_1$ inside $DL'$ for the same reason as above, with the boundary component taking the place of $\alpha$. This rules out all possibilities for a periodic curve $\gamma_i$, and we conclude that $Df'_\varphi$ is atoroidal.


    Since $Df_\varphi'$ is an atoroidal, endperiodic map on a surface with no boundary components and with all ends nonplanar, it is isotopic to some spun pseudo-Anosov map $g$ by \cite{landry2023endperiodic}. By \cite[Lemma 5.13]{landry2023endperiodic}, either $g$ has a periodic point  or $g$ is a translation. The latter case is precisely the case that $N$, and hence $U$, are topological products. By hypothesis we conclude $g$ has a periodic point, and by \cite{landry2023endperiodic} $Df'_\varphi$ must also have a periodic point. Since the periodic points of $f'_\varphi$ correspond 2-to-1 exactly to those of $f_\varphi$, $f_\varphi$ has a periodic point and we are done.
head: environment

label: lem:approxedimpliesforcing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:approxedimpliesforcing}
	If $\mathcal F$ is $C^0$-approximated by foliations which force closed orbits, then $\mathcal F$ forces closed orbits.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $\mathcal F$ be a $C^0$ foliation, and let $\{\mathcal F_i\}_{i\in N}$ be a sequence of foliations which force closed orbits such that $T \mathcal F_i$ converges to $T \mathcal F$ in the $C^0$ topology. Let $\varphi$ be a flow transverse to $\mathcal F$. Since transversality is an open condition, past some $N\in \mathbb{N}$ we have that $\varphi\pitchfork\mathcal F_i$. Since $\mathcal F_i$ forces closed orbits, $\varphi$ has a closed orbit.
head: environment

label: cor:no holonomy again
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:no holonomy again}
	If $\mathcal F$ is $C^2$ and has no holonomy, then $\mathcal F$ forces closed orbits.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Tischler's Theorem \cite{candel_foliations_1999} implies that $\mathcal F$ is $C^0$ approximated by fibrations; since $M$ is atoroidal, these fibrations are not fibrations by tori, and so they force closed orbits. Since $\mathcal F$ is a $C^0$-limit of foliations forcing closed orbits, Lemma \ref{lem:approxedimpliesforcing} implies $\mathcal F$ forces closed orbits.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Our definition is slightly different from the one appearing in the literature, e.g. \cite{hurder_dynamics_2015}. The primary difference is that we have dropped the \textbf{\emph{tameness condition}}, that the plug embeds into $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserving the vertical direction at the boundary. Our plug insertions will not occur in small coordinate balls, and so this hypothesis is not necessary. Nonetheless, all known plugs satisfy this condition.
head: environment

label: lem:pluginsertion
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Plug Insertion

label: lem:insertion1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi$, $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, and $L$ be as in the lemma statement. Fix a neighborhood $U$ of $\gamma_1 \cup \gamma_2$ in $M$. Pick $\varepsilon$ small enough such that \[\varphi^{[0,\varepsilon]}(\gamma_1 \cup \gamma_2) \subset U,\] and
 the holonomy along $\gamma_1$ is defined and attracting along the entire transversal $\varphi^{[0, \varepsilon]}(x)$ for any $x$ in $\gamma_1$. 
 We now take a small tubular neighborhood $V \subset U$ of $\gamma_1 \cup \gamma_2$ in $L$ so that $\varphi^{[0, \varepsilon]}(\overline{V}) \subset U$. By switching the orientation of $\gamma_2$ if necessary, we can choose a diffeomorphism 
    \[
    h\colon S\to \overline{V}
    \]
    taking $\gamma_h$ to $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_v$ to $\gamma_2$. This gives an embedding 
    \[
    i_0\colon P_0\to U,
    \] 
    where $P_0=S\times[0,1]$, by the formula 
    \[ 
    i_0(x, t) = \varphi^{\varepsilon t}(h(x)). 
    \]
    We pull back $\mathcal{F}$ along $i_0$ to obtain a foliation $\mathcal G$ on $P_0$. We henceforth work in $P_0$ and consider the holonomy along curves or arcs in $S$ as acting on relatively open intervals $[0, 1]$ containing $0$.
    
    Observe that $\mathcal G$ has attracting holonomy along $\gamma_h$. Therefore, there is some $n$ such that $\gamma_v\gamma^n_h$ has attracting holonomy in the interval $[1/4, 3/4]$. Fixing $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, and recall that the train track $\tau_n$ carries $K_\alpha$. 

	We now define a lift of $\tau_n$ from $S$ to $P_0$, transverse to $\mathcal G$, as follows. First recall that $\tau_n = \gamma_h \cup c_n$, and $\gamma_h\cap c_n$ is an arc $a$ not containing $(-1,-1)$. We begin by lifting $(-1, -1)$ to $(-1, -1, 1/2)$ and proceed in the forward direction along $\gamma_h$ using parallel transport for $\mathcal G$, obtaining a lift of $\gamma_h$ to a leaf of $\mathcal G$ which is continuous except at $(-1,-1)$. This is possible since $\mathcal G$ has attracting holonomy along $\gamma_h$ on the entire interval $[0,1]$. Let 
	\[
	f\colon \gamma_h\to[0,1]
	\]
	be the height function for this lift.
	
	Next, isotope $\tau_n$ in $S$ such that $a^-$, the negative endpoint of the arc $a$, is close enough to $(-1,-1)$ to satisfy
	\[
	f(a^-)\in(1/4,3/4).
	\]
	Now start lifting $c_n$ to $P_0$, starting by lifting $a^-$ to $(a^-,f(a^-))$, and continuing along $c_n$ in the forward direction via parallel transport for $\mathcal G$ as with $\gamma_h$. This extends the lift of $\gamma_h$ to a lift of $\tau_n$, contained in a single leaf of $\mathcal G$, where we now have discontinuities over both $(-1,-1)$ and $a^-$. Abusing notation, we now let $f$ denote the height function of this lift on all of $\tau_n$.
	
	To remedy these discontinuities, and to make the lift of $\tau_n$ transverse to $\mathcal G$, we `tilt' the lift up as we move in the forward direction along $\gamma_h$ and $c_n$ as follows. Since $\gamma_h$ has attracting holonomy at $1/2$, the limit of $f$ approaching $(-1, -1)$ in the forward direction along $\gamma_h$ is less than $1/2$. Similarly, since $f(a^-)\in(1/4,3/4)$, the holonomy along $c_n$ is defined and attracting at $f(a^-)$, so the limit of $f$ approaching $a^-$ in the forward direction along $c_n$ is less than $f(a^-)$. Thus, we can define a function
	\[
	E\colon \tau_n\to[0,1]
	\]
	which is $0$ at $(-1,-1)$ and $a^-$, has discontinuities at exactly these points, is otherwise smooth and monotonely increasing along the positive directions of $\gamma_h$ and $c_n$, and such that
	\[
	f+E\colon \tau_n\to [0,1]
	\]
	gives a height function for a smooth lift of $\tau_n$ to $P_0$ transverse to $\mathcal G$. Let
	\[
	\tilde{f}\colon\tau_n\to P_0
	\]
	denote this lift.

    Extend $\tilde{f}$ to a small tie neighborhood $N_\delta = N_\delta(\tau_n)$ of $\tau_n$ in $S$ so that the graph of $N_\delta$ is transverse to $\mathcal{G}$ and the intersection foliation defines a foliation by ties of $N_\delta$. Let $$q: S \to S$$ be a diffeomorphism of $S$ isotopic to the identity which takes $K_\alpha$ into $N_\delta$ transverse to this foliation by ties. Then the graph of $q(K_\alpha)$ under $\tilde{f}$ is transverse to $\mathcal G$. Let $$r: P^+_{\alpha, \psi} \to P_0$$ be a diffeomorphism which preserves the interval fibers in the vertical direction and takes $K_\alpha \times \{1/2\}$ to the graph of $q(K_\alpha)$ under $\tilde{f}$, and define $i = i_0 \circ r$. Then for a bump function $\psi$ with sufficiently small support, $$i: P^+_{\alpha, \psi} \to U$$ defines the desired semiplug insertion. Note that the point $x$ lies in $\tau_n$, and so we may choose the isotopy of $K_\alpha$ into a neighborhood of $\tau_n$ so that $x$ lies in $K_\alpha$.

    In the case that $\gamma_1$ has attracting holonomy on both sides, choose $n$ large enough that $\gamma_2\gamma^n_1$ has an interval of attracting holonomy on both sides, and perform the same construction to obtain a negative semiplug insertion $i_-: P^-_{\alpha, \psi} \to U$. Choose the same $\psi$ for both constructions. By modifying $i_-$ via an isotopy near $L$, the images of $K_\alpha$ can be chosen to match up and the union of the positive and negative semiplugs defines a full Schweitzer plug insertion.
head: environment

label: lem:pluginsertion again
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Plug Insertion

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi$, $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, $L$, $U$, and $C$ be as in the lemma statement. Let $R$ be a compact region in $U\cap L$ containing $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, and a small open neighborhood around $C$, and homeomorphic to $T^2\setminus D$. Similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:insertion1}, let $\varepsilon>0$ be small enough so that 
	\[
	\varphi^{[0,\varepsilon]}(R)\subset U,
	\]
	and the holonomy along $\gamma_1$ is defined and attracting along the entire transversal $\varphi^{[0,\varepsilon]}(z)$ for any $z$ in $\gamma_1$.  Proceeding with the rest of the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:insertion1}, taking $V\subset U$ to contain $R$, produces an unmodified Schweitzer plug insertion
	\[
	i_0\colon P_{\alpha, \psi} \to M
	\]
	contained in $U$, and whose image contains $C$.
	
	In $P_{\alpha,\psi}$, we may blow up $K$ around $x$ to obtain a modified Schweitzer plug insertion 
	\[ 
	i\colon P = P_{\alpha, x, \psi} \to M.
	\]
	Choose this blowup to be small enough that the plugged flow is still transverse to $\mathcal{F}$. This is possible since transversality is an open condition. 
	
	What remains to be shown is that we can change $i$ so that all orbits through $C$ are trapped by the new plug. To achieve this, we `funnel' the orbits through $C$ into the trapped set of $P$ as follows. Let $C'$ be a small closed disk contained in the trapped set of $P$. 
	Let $D$ be an open disk in $L\cap i(P)$ containing $C$ and $C'$, and fix a neighborhood $B\cong D\times[-1,1]$ such that the vertical $[-1,1]$ fibers are flowlines of $\varphi$. By reparametrizing the flowline coordinates of $B$ and extending $P$ along flowlines, we may assume that the disks $D \times \{\pm 1/2\}$ form the positive and negative boundary of $i(P) \cap B$ and that $\mathcal F$ restricts to a product foliation in $D \times [1/2 - \delta, 1/2]$ and $D \times [-1/2, -1/2 + \delta]$, where $\delta>0$ is chosen small enough that these regions are outside of $i(\text{supp}(\psi))$.
	
	Let $\pi\colon B\to D$ be the projection map along flow lines, and let 
	\(
	h_t\colon D\to D
	\)
	for $t\in[0,\delta]$ be an isotopy such that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $h_0$ is the identity,
		\item $h_\delta(\pi(C))\subset \pi(C')$,
		\item $h_t=h_0$ for $t$ close to $0$, and 
		\item $h_t=h_\delta$ for $t$ close to $\delta$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
    Then define a map $H:B\to B$ by 
    \[H(z, t) = \begin{cases}
    (h_{ t - (\frac 1 2 - \delta)}(z),t) & t \in [1/2 - \delta, 1/2]\\
    (h_{t - (\delta - \frac 1 2)}(z),t) & t \in [-1/2, -1/2 + \delta]\\
    (z, t) & \text{ otherwise.}
    \end{cases}\]
    Then $H \circ i: P \to M$ is the desired plug insertion.
head: environment

label: lem:annularpluginsertion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:annularpluginsertion}
	Suppose $L_-$ and $L_+$ cobound a topological product $L_- \times [0, 1]$ and $\varphi$ is a flow transverse to $\mathcal F$ which defines a dynamical product between $L_-$ and $L_+$. Suppose $A$ is an annulus of attracting holonomy between them which is tangent to $\varphi$. Let $\gamma$ be an oriented simple closed curve in $L_-$ such that $\partial_- A$ and $\gamma$ intersect positively and transversely at a single point.
	Then for any neighborhood $U$ of $\gamma \times [0, 1] \cup A$ in $M$ for which $\varphi$ is smooth, there is a modified Schweitzer plug insertion 
	\[
	i:P = P_{\alpha,x, \psi'} \to U
	\] 
	such that the plugged flow $\varphi_P$ is transverse to $\mathcal F$. Moreover, if $C$ is any closed disk contained in 
	\[
	N\left(\gamma \times [0, 1] \cup A\right) \cap L_-,
	\]
	where $N\left(\gamma \times [0, 1]\cup A\right)$ is a normal neighborhood of $\gamma \times [0, 1]\cup A$, then the insertion can be chosen so that all orbits passing through $C$ are trapped by $P$.
head: environment
name: Annular Plug Insertion Lemma

label: thm:perturb again
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:perturb again}
	 If every leaf of $\mathcal F$ has genus, then $\mathcal F$ can be $C^0$-approximated by foliations which do not force closed orbits.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose every leaf of $\mathcal F$ has genus, and let $\varphi$ be a smooth flow transverse to $\mathcal{F}$. By compactness of $M$, we may find a finite collection $\{C_j\}_{j=1,\ldots,n}$ of closed disks such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item each $C_j$ is contained in a distinct leaf $L_j$ of $\mathcal F$, and
        \item every closed orbit of $\varphi$ intersects at least one $C_j$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Let $\{D_j\}_{j=1,\ldots,n}$ be a finite collection of open disks such that 
    \[
    C_j\subset D_j\subset L_j
    \]
    for all $j$, and flow out each $D_j$ slightly along $\varphi$ to a disjoint collection $\{V_j\}$ of foliated flowbox neighborhoods. For each $j$, let $\gamma_j$ be a nonseparating simple closed curve in $L_j$. Such a curve is guaranteed to exist since each leaf of $\mathcal F$ has genus.

    We now construct a new foliation $\mathcal F'$ by blowing up each $L_j$ and inserting the following foliation. On $L_j \times [-1, 1]$, consider the product foliation by copies of $L_j$, and take a simple closed curve $\alpha_j$ in $L_j \times \{0\}$ which intersects $\gamma_j \times \{0\}$ transversely in a single point. Such an $\alpha_j$ exists since $\gamma_j$ is nonseparating. Now shear along the annuli $\alpha_j \times [-1, 0]$ and $\alpha_j \times [0, 1]$ so that $\gamma_j \times \{0\}$ has attracting holonomy. Call this foliation $\mathcal F_j$. Then $\mathcal F'$ is obtained as a generalized Denjoy blowup of $\mathcal F$ along the leaves $L_j$, inserting the foliations $\mathcal F_j$ as saturated sets $U_j$ for all $j$. By \cite[Theorem 5.2]{kazez_c0_2017}, this foliation can be chosen to be $C^0$-close to $\mathcal F$. In particular, under this construction $\varphi$ will still be transverse to $\mathcal F'$. 
    
    Abusing notation, we refer to the leaf in $\mathcal F'$ corresponding to $L_j \times \{0\}$ in $F_j$ as $L_j$. Furthermore, we consider $D_j$ and $\gamma_j$ as lying in $L_j \times \{0\}$. Note the collection $\{C_j\}$ still intersects each closed orbit of $\varphi$. 
    
    By Lemma \ref{lem:pluginsertion} we may insert modified Schweitzer plugs $\{P_j\}_{j=1,\ldots,n}$ which trap all the closed orbits passing through $C_j$. These insertions can be chosen to lie in the blowup regions $U_j$ and therefore are disjoint. The resulting plugged flow, $\varphi'$, will be the desired $C^1$ aperiodic flow.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:base region structure}
	Let $U$ be a base region of base depth $\ell$ for the foliation $\mathcal F$. For $d\geq \ell$, let 
	\[
	V_d=\{L\;\mid\;L\text{  a leaf in }U\text{ of depth }\geq d\}.
	\]
	Then the following hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $U$ is not a product region.
		\item $\mathcal F\mid_U$ is obtained from $\check{\mathcal F}\mid_U$ by iterated shearing in product regions.
		\item If $d>\ell$, $V_d$ is a collection of open product regions $V_d^i$, each of the form \[\Sigma^i\times (0,1)\] for $\Sigma^i$ a leaf of $\mathcal F\mid_U$ of depth $d-1$, and the foliation on $V_d^i$ is obtained from the product foliation by iterated shearing. Furthermore, $V_d^i$ is a mapping torus region.
	\end{enumerate}

title: Definition
body_md:

\[
j^+(L) = -j^-(L).
\]
Say a mapping torus component $V$ in $U$ has \textbf{\emph{connecting junctures}} if every leaf realising the fiber depth does. Say $U$ has \textbf{\emph{connecting junctures}} if all mapping torus components of $U$ do.

label: prop:C2connectinghasdepth1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:C2connectinghasdepth1}
	Suppose $U$ is a base region of depth $k$ and base depth $\ell$. If $U$ has connecting, compactly supported junctures, then $U$ has relative depth at most one.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ be a base region of depth $k$ and base depth $\ell$, and suppose $U$ has compactly supported junctures. Suppose that $U$ has relative depth higher than one, i.e. $k-\ell>1$. 
	
	Let 
	\[
	V_{k-1}=\{L\;\mid\;L\text{ a leaf in }U\text{ of depth }\geq k-1\},
	\]
	as in Lemma \ref{lem:base region structure}. Suppose for simplicity that $V_{k-1}$ is connected; the same argument applies to each connected component of $V_{k-1}$. Since $k-1>\ell$, we have that $V_{k-1}$ is not all of $U$, and is instead a product region of the form 
	\[
	\Sigma\times(0,1)
	\]
	for $\Sigma$ a leaf of $\mathcal F\mid_U$ of depth $k-2$ by Lemma \ref{lem:base region structure}. Furthermore, $V_{k-1}$ fibers over $S^1$ with fiber $L_{k-1}$, a leaf of depth $k-1$ in $V_{k-1}$.
	
	Since $U$ has compactly supported junctures, the monodromy 
	\[
	f\colon L_{k-1}\to L_{k-1}
	\]
	for the fibration structure above is a generalized endperiodic map. Furthermore, $f$ is homotopic to a translation, since the mapping torus is a topological product. Thus, $f$ has no eigenvectors on $H^1_c(L_{k-1})$, the compactly supported cohomology of $L_{k-1}$.
	
	On the other hand, we now claim that if $U$ has connecting junctures, then the map $f$ \emph{does} have an eigenvector on $H^1_c(L_{k-1})$. Suppose toward contradiction that $U$ has connecting junctures. Within $V_{k-1}$, the depth $k$ leaves are contained in saturated mapping tori of the form 
	\[
	L_{k-1}\times (0,1),
	\]
	and these are divided by depth $k-1$ trivially foliated products of the form
	\[
	L_{k-1}\times [0,1].
	\]
	Label these regions as 
	\[
	W_1',W_1,W_2',W_2,\ldots,W_r', W_r,
	\]
	where the $W_i'$ are the depth $k-1$ regions, the $W_i$ are the depth $k$ regions, and consecutive indices correspond to adjacent regions, ordered cyclically to agree with coorientation. 
	
	Let $\varphi$ be a transverse flow on $V_{k-1}$ turning each $W_i'$ into a dynamical product, and use this flow to blow down each $W_i'$ into a single leaf
	\[
	L^i\cong L_{k-1}.
	\]
	Note now that the positive and negative boundary components of $\widehat W_i$ are $L^i$ and $L^{i+1}$ respectively, with indices taken mod $r$.
    
	For each $i$, let $\gamma_i$ be a representative in $H_1(L^i)$ of the Poincar\'e dual of $j^+(L^i)$. This $\gamma_i$ can be chosen to be a compact, immersed 1-manifold since the junctures are compactly supported. Let 
	\[
	A_i = \gamma_i \times [0,1],
	\]
	where we identify $\widehat W_i$ with $L^i \times [0, 1]$. Then $A_i$ is an immersed annulus with boundary 
	\[
	-\gamma \times \{0\} \sqcup \gamma \times \{1\}.
	\]
	Its positive boundary is a representative of $j^-(L^{i+1})$. Denote $\partial_- A_i = -\gamma \times \{0\}$ and $\partial_+ A_i = \gamma \times\{1\}$.
	
	Since the junctures connect, modulo $n$ we have that 
	\[
	[\partial_- A_i] = [\partial_+ A_{i-1}] \in H_1(L^i).
	\] 
	Therefore we can connect them with compact immersed subsurfaces $S^i$ contained in $L^i$. These close up to a closed, homologically nontrivial surface in $V$, so the Poincar\'e dual of the juncture class provides an eigenvector of the monodromy on $H_1(L_{k-1})$. Since the junctures are compactly supported, this gives an eigenvector in $H^1_c(L_{k-1})$. This produces the desired contradiction.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Keeping the notation of the proof above, a similar argument shows that if $V_{k-1}$ has connecting junctures which are not compactly supported, then the monodromy has an eigenvector on $H^1(L_{k-1})$. However, translations have many such eigenvectors, and so this phenomenon does indeed occur. The surface representatives now lie in $H_2(\widehat V_{k-1}, \partial \widehat V_{k-1})$.

label: lem:connectingapproxfinite
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connectingapproxfinite}
	Suppose $U$ is a base region of $\mathcal F$ of relative depth at most one. Then in $U$, $\mathcal F$ can be approximated by fibrations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $U$ is a base region of relative depth zero, it is a locally top-depth component and the result follows from Lemma \ref{lem:top depth is fibered}. So, let $U$ be a base region of $\mathcal F$ of relative depth one. Fix a smooth flow $\varphi$ transverse to $\mathcal F$ and defining a dynamical product on every product region. Let $N$ be an immersed carrying sutured manifold for $U$, as given by the Octopus Decomposition Lemma \ref{lem:octopus}. Enlarging $N$ if necessary, we assume the restriction of $\mathcal F$ to $\partial_\pitchfork N$ is a trivial foliation by circles. This is possible since there are finitely many locally top-depth components in $U$, and each one has compact junctures. We work in $\widehat N$, where $\mathcal F$ pulls back to a foliation $\mathcal G$. Since $U$ is relative depth one, the foliation $\mathcal G$ is depth two.

	As above, let $L_0, ..., L_n$ be depth one fiber leaves separating the top-depth regions $W_1, ..., W_n$ in $\mathcal G$. For each positive juncture $j^+(L_i)$, choose a compact, embedded 1-manifold realization $m_i$. Since the junctures connect, we can take $-m_i$ as a representative of $j^-(L_i)$. 
	
	We now truncate the depth 2 leaves in each $W_i$ and push them into $L_i$ as follows. Let $S_i$ be a fiber leaf of $W_i$, take a large subsurface $S_i'\subset S_i$, and push the negative boundary slightly along $\varphi$ into $L_i$ and push the positive boundary into $L_{i+1}$ (modulo $n$). Each $S_i$ has finitely many ends parallel to each end of $L_i$, some number of boundary components meeting $\partial_\pitchfork N$ tangent to $\mathcal G$, and compact negative and positive boundary components  lying in $L_{i}$ and $L_{i+1}$, respectively. As in \cite[Lemma 3.7]{landry2023endperiodic}, following ideas of Gabai \cite[Lemma 0.6]{Gabai1987} , we may choose these $S_i'$ so that the boundary is precisely $-m_i \cup m_{i+1}$, and so each $S_i'$ glues up (along with product annuli $m_i \times [0,1]$ for each $L_i$ which lies in a product region) to obtain a compact surface $\Sigma$. 
	
	Taking a sequence of such $\{S_{i_j}'\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ exhausting each $S_i$, we obtain a sequence $\{\Sigma_j\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ of surfaces as above with boundary tangent to $\mathcal G$ in $\partial_\pitchfork N$. For sufficiently large $j$, each $\Sigma_j$ intersects every orbit of $\varphi$ infinitely many times and hence is a fiber of a fibration $\mathcal G_k$ of the interior of $N$, tangent to $\mathcal G$ along $\partial_\pitchfork N$. The boundary condition allows us to modify $\mathcal F$ in the interior of $N$ to a foliation $\mathcal F_j$ which is a fibration in $U$. The foliations $\mathcal F_j$ $C^0$-converge to $\mathcal F$, as desired.

label: lem:connectingholonomyfinite
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connectingholonomyfinite}
	Suppose $\mathcal F$ is $C^2$ and has no toral leaves, and let $U$ be a base region of $\mathcal F$. If $U$ does not have connecting junctures, then $U$ has a leaf $L$ with a nonseparating curve of two-sided attracting holonomy or has an annulus of attracting holonomy.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal F$ and $U$ be as in the lemma statement, and let $L$ be a depth $i$ leaf realizing the fact that $U$ does not have connecting junctures, i.e. $L$ satisfies
	\[
	j^+(L) \neq -j^-(L)\;\;\text{in}\; \; H^1(L,\mathbb{R}),
	\]
	possibly after identifying $L$ with a leaf cobounding a trivially foliated product with $L$. If this is the case, blow down that product so that $L$ is isolated in the set of depth $i$ leaves.
	
	Since $\mathcal F$ is $C^2$ and has no toral leaves, all leaves of positive depth have all ends accumulated by genus by \cite[Corollary 8.4.7]{candel_foliations_1999}. In particular, no matter the depth, the dimension of $H_1(L, \mathbb{R})$ is at least 2. The classes $j^+(L)$ and $j^-(L)$ both define linear functionals on $H_1(L, \mathbb{R})$. The open half-spaces 
	\[
	P^\pm = \{a \in H_1(L, \mathbb{R}) \mid j^\pm(a) > 0\}
	\]
	have nonempty intersection if and only if $j^+(L) \neq -j^-(L)$. Therefore there is a nonempty open cone $C = P^+ \cap P^-$ such that any simple closed curve with homology class lying in $C$ has attracting holonomy.
	
	We now claim we can find such a curve which is nonseparating. Since the junctures of $\mathcal F$ are compactly supported, any simple closed curve whose homology class lies in $C$ must have positive signed count of intersections with a compact representative of the Poincar\'e duals of the junctures $j^\pm(L)$, and so is nonseparating. Since $C$ is open, we can find a primitive integral homology class to obtain the desired curve.
	
	If $L$ did not lie on the boundary of a trivially foliated product, we have produced a curve of two-sided attracting holonomy and are done. Otherwise, blow the product region back up and observe that the preimage under the blowup of the curve of attracting holonomy is an annulus of attracting holonomy.
head: environment

label: lem:holonomy implies not fibr
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:holonomy implies not fibr}
	Suppose a base region $U$ has a curve or annulus of two-sided attracting holonomy. Then it is not approximated by fibrations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ be a base region for a foliation $\mathcal F$, and let $\gamma$ be a curve of attracting holonomy (or be a core curve of an annulus of attracting holonomy). Suppose toward contradiction that $\mathcal F\mid_U$ is approximated by a sequence $\{\mathcal F_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of fibrations in $U$. 
	
	By the assumption on $\gamma$, it is isotopic in $U$ to a curve positively transverse to $\mathcal F$ and hence positively transverse to $\mathcal F_i$ for $i$ sufficiently large. Likewise, it is isotopic in $U$ to a curve negatively transverse to $\mathcal F$ and hence negatively transverse to $\mathcal F_i$ for $i$ sufficiently large. This is a contradiction since the $\mathcal F_i$ are fibrations in $U$.

body_md: For the remainder of this section, fix a smooth flow $\varphi$ transverse to $\mathcal F$ defining a dynamical product on every product region.

title: Definition
body_md:
Say that the mapping torus component $V$ has \textbf{\emph{connecting (limit) junctures}} if for all $a \in A$, 
	\[
	J^+(\Sigma_a) = -J^-(\Sigma_a)\hspace{1cm}\text{and}\hspace{1cm}|J^+(\Sigma_a)| = |J^-(\Sigma_a)| = 1.
	\]
	Say the base region $U$ has \textbf{\emph{connecting (limit) junctures}} if all mapping torus components of $U$ do.

label: lem:connectingimpliesconstant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connectingimpliesconstant}
	Suppose $U$ has relative depth one and has connecting limit junctures, and let $N$ be a closed topological product with distinct relative depth zero negative and positive boundary leaves $\Sigma_-$ and $\Sigma_+$. Then under the homeomorphism $\Sigma_- \cong \Sigma_+$ induced by sliding along flow lines of $\varphi$ in $N$, $J^-(\Sigma_-) = -J^+(\Sigma_+)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We can index the relative depth zero leaves of $\mathcal F$ in $N$ by a set $A_N$, which we consider as a subset of a flowline of $\varphi$ with the subspace topology, which we in turn identify with the interval $[0, 1]$.
	
	We consider the limit junctures $J^\pm$ as functions $A_N \to H^1(\Sigma_-)$. We claim that by the connecting limit junctures hypothesis, for every $x \in A_N$ there is an open neighborhood $B_x$ such that $J^-$ (and hence also $J^+$) is constant. Let $\{y_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq A_N$ be a sequence converging to $x$. By passing to a subsequence, either all $y_i < x$ or all $y_i > x$. First suppose $y_i < x$. Then there is a sequence $z_i \to x$ such that each $z_i$ is isolated on the negative side and $J^-(z_i) = J^-(y_i)$. Now since $J^-(x)$ is a singleton, by the definition of limit junctures $J^-(z_i)$ is eventually constant.
	
	On the other hand, suppose $x < y_i$ for all $i$. Then there is a sequence $w_i$ converging to $x$ such that each $w_i$ is isolated on the negative side and $J^-(y_i) = J^-(w_i)$ for all $i$. Each $w_i$ cobounds a gap with some point $t_i$, and so by Lemma \ref{lem:juncturesinproduct}, $J^-(w_i) = j^-(w_i) = -j^+(t_i) = -J^+(t_i)$. However, for $t_i$ close enough to $x$, since all junctures are singletons, $-J^+(t_i) = -J^+(x) = J^-(x)$, applying the connecting junctures hypothesis. Therefore, for sufficiently large $i$, $J^-(y_i) = J^-(x)$. This shows that $J^-$ is locally constant.
	
	To conclude that a function on a subset of a Cantor set in $[0, 1]$ is constant, it suffices to show that it is both locally constant and that its values on endpoints of gaps are equal. But the latter claim follows again by Lemma \ref{lem:juncturesinproduct} and the connecting junctures hypothesis. Therefore $J^-$ (and hence also $J^+$) is constant on $A_N$. This concludes the proof.
head: environment

label: prop:connecting implies rel depth 1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:connecting implies rel depth 1}
	Suppose $U$ has compactly supported junctures and connecting limit junctures. Then $U$ has relative depth at most one.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof is exactly the same as in the finite case; the connecting limit junctures hypothesis allows us to build a homology class in a connected relative depth one region $V$ topologically fibering over $S^1$ with generalized endperiodic monodromy. Choose a single locally top-depth region and use Lemma \ref{lem:connectingimpliesconstant} to insert annuli in the other product regions with boundaries representing the junctures of the finitely many chosen locally top-depth regions. This gives the desired homologically nontrivial closed surface in $V$.
head: environment

label: lem:connectingapproxinfinite
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connectingapproxinfinite}
	Suppose $U$ is a base region of relative depth at most one, has compactly supported junctures, and has connecting limit junctures. Then in $U$, $\mathcal F$ can be approximated by fibrations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $U$ be as in the lemma statement. We show that in $U$, $\mathcal F$ can be $C^0$-approximated by a foliation with finitely many locally top-depth components and connecting junctures. In some Riemannian metric, since $U$ has infinitely many locally top-depth regions, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ it has locally top-depth regions $V$ such that every orbit segment of $\varphi$ contained in $V$ has length less than $\varepsilon$. Then in all such $V$ we replace $\mathcal F$ with a product foliation. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, we get a sequence $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$ of foliations with finitely many locally top-depth regions in $U$ which approaches $\mathcal F$.
	
	For a fixed $\varepsilon$, let $V_\varepsilon$ be the union of all of these new product regions and let $N$ be a connected component of its closure. For $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, $N$ is not all of $U$. Then $N$ is a trivially foliated product region, and its positive and negative boundary components $\Sigma_+$ and $\Sigma_-$ bound gaps of $A$, the index set for the lowest depth leaves in $U$. By Lemma \ref{lem:connectingimpliesconstant}, $J_-(\Sigma_-) = -J_+(\Sigma_+)$ in $\mathcal F$, and since we have only replace leaves in the interior of $N$ this also holds for $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$. Therefore, we see that $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$ has connecting junctures. Since $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$ has finitely many locally top-depth regions, we may apply Lemma \ref{lem:connectingapproxfinite} to conclude that in $U$, $\mathcal F_\varepsilon$ is approximated by fibrations. Finally, a diagonal argument shows $\mathcal F$ is approximated by fibrations in $U$.
head: environment

label: lem:connectingholonomyinfinite
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connectingholonomyinfinite}
	Suppose $U$ does not have connecting limit junctures. Then $U$ has a nonseparating curve or annulus of attracting holonomy.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $U$ does not have connecting limit junctures, there is some leaf $S$ with $J^+(S) \neq -J^-(S)$. If $S$ is isolated, this is the standard juncture and the argument is the same as in Lemma \ref{lem:connectingholonomyfinite}. If $S$ is not isolated, then by the definition of limit junctures there are leaves $S_-, S_+$, with $S_- \leq S \leq S_+$ in the local coorientation order, such that $S_-$ (resp. $S_+$) is isolated on the negative (resp. positive) side, and under the identifications of their homologies in the product neighborhood they cobound, $j^-(S_-) \neq -j^+(S_+)$. The same argument as in the finite case gives a nonseparating annulus of attracting holonomy.

label: prop:junctures capstone again
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth and $C^2$, and let $U$ be a base region. Suppose first that $U$ has connecting (limit) junctures. Then Proposition \ref{prop:connecting implies rel depth 1} implies $U$ has relative depth one, and Lemma \ref{lem:connectingapproxinfinite} applies to show $\mathcal F$ is approximated by fibrations in $U$.
	
	On the other hand, if $U$ does not have connecting (limit) junctures, then Lemma \ref{lem:connectingholonomyinfinite} produces the desired curve or annulus of attracting holonomy.

label: lem:smaleisdense
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{lem:smaleisdense}
    Any smooth vector field is $C^0$-close to a smooth vector field generating a Smale flow.
head: environment

label: thm:characterization again
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Characterization Theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth and $C^2$. Let $U_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ be the base regions of $\mathcal F$. If any $U_i$ has connecting (limit) junctures, then by Proposition \ref{prop:junctures capstone}, $\mathcal F$ can be approximated by fibrations $\{\mathcal F_j\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $U_i$. By Lemma \ref{lem:base region structure}, $U_i$ is not a product region. Thus, Theorem \ref{thm:locallytopdepthclosing} implies each $\mathcal F_j$ forces closed orbits. Finally, Lemma \ref{lem:approxedimpliesforcing} implies $\mathcal F$ forces closed orbits in $U_i$, as it is approximated there by foliations that force closed orbits. 
    
    Suppose instead that each $U_i$ has junctures which don't connect. Then there is a leaf $L_i$ in each $U_i$ which either has a nonseparating curve $\gamma_i$ of attracting holonomy, or cobounds a topological product with a leaf $L_i'$ and has an annulus of attracting holonomy which restricts to a nonseparating curve in $L_i$. Let $\varphi_0$ be  a smooth flow which defines a dynamical product on every topological product region in $\mathcal F$. For each $i$, any closed orbit of $\varphi_0$ intersecting $U_i$ must intersect every leaf of $U_i$. This is because $\varphi_0$ defines a suspension flow on $U_i$ with fiber any relative depth zero leaf, and all higher depth leaves accumulate on these leaves. Note also that every closed orbit of $\varphi_0$ must intersect some $U_i$, as open sets in the complement of the base regions are all contained in product regions. From this we see that every closed orbit of $\varphi_0$ intersects some $L_i$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:smaleisdense}, we can $C^0$-approximate $\varphi_0$ by a Smale flow $\varphi$ which must also have the property that every closed orbit intersects some $L_i$.
    
    Let $C$ be the closure of the set of closed orbits of $\varphi$. Then the set $C$ intersects each $L_i$ in a union of totally disconnected sets. Since $M$ is compact, each $L_i$ has a compact subsurface $S_i$ such that every closed orbit of $\varphi$ intersects some $S_i$. We can choose $S_i$ so that its boundary is disjoint from $C$, and therefore we can find a closed disk $D_i$ in each $S_i$ that contains $C \cap S_i$ in its interior. In particular, every closed orbit of $\varphi$ intersects some $D_i$.

    If $L_i$ has a curve of attracting holonomy, then by Lemma \ref{lem:pluginsertion} we may insert a plug $P_i$ in a small neighborhood of $L_i$ so that $D_i$ is trapped by the plug. Choose the neighborhood small enough so that the image of $P_i$ is contained in the base region $U_i$.

    If $L_i$ cobounds a topological product region with $L_i'$ and has an annulus of attracting holonomy. Then since $\varphi$ defines a dynamical product on every product region, we may similarly use Lemma \ref{lem:annularpluginsertion} to insert a plug $P_i$ trapped all orbits intersecting $D_i$.

    Let $\varphi'$ be the plugged flow after inserting the plugs $P_i$ for all $i$. These plug insertions are disjoint, so no new closed orbits are created with each plug insertion. Every orbit in $C$ is trapped by some $P_i$. Therefore, $\varphi'$ is an aperiodic flow transverse to $\mathcal F$. Since we have inserted $C^{1}$ plugs into a $C^\infty$ flow, $\varphi'$ is generated by a $C^{1}$ vector field, as desired. This concludes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:blowdown again
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:blowdown again}
	Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth. If $\mathcal F$ does not force closed orbits, then it is obtained by iterated shearing of a foliation that does.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite depth. Let $\check{\mathcal F}$ be the foliation defined in Section \ref{subsec:base regions}, i.e. the foliation obtained from $\mathcal F$ by iteratively replacing locally top-depth components that are topological products with trivially foliated products. Then by Lemma \ref{lem:base region structure}, every locally top-depth component of $\check{\mathcal F}$ is not a topological product, and so $\check{\mathcal F}$ forces closed orbits by Theorem \ref{thm:locallytopdepthclosing}. By Lemma \ref{lem:base region structure}, $\mathcal F$ is obtained from $\check{\mathcal F}$ by iterated shearing, and this completes the proof.
head: environment
